newsitem.title: INDIA: Voices of Gandhi, Nehru mark India's birthday.
newsitem.headline: Voices of Gandhi, Nehru mark India's birthday.

text.p: India invoked Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru on Friday in a midnight tribute to the nation's freedom struggle and half century of independence.
The voices of Gandhi and Nehru echoed through parliament in a sombre ceremony 50 years to the minute since India won freedom from two centuries of British colonial rule.

"Long years ago we made a tryst with destiny, and now the time comes when we shall redeem our pledge, not wholly or in full measure, but very substantially," India's first prime minister, Nehru, said in a recording of his speech at midnight August 14-15 1947 in the same hall.
"At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom."
President K.R. Narayanan eagerly took up the famous theme.
"This midnight hour, thronged with memories of the past and throbbing with significance for the future, is a golden moment in he history of India and the world," the president said.

The 45-minute midnight session closed an evening's activities to begin a year of celebrations honouring the fight against British rule that ended in India's freedom and the partition of the subcontinent.
India's neighbouring arch-rival, Pakistan, celebrated its 50th anniversary of independence on Thursday, but the festive mood was soured by crowd trouble at a rally in Karachi.

Two people were killed by gunfire and a score injured in a stampede after Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif addressed a crowd of about 20,000 at the marble mausoleum of the Islamic state's founder, Mohammad Ali Jinnah, in the southern port city.
India's own lavish celebrations were tinged with sorrow as citizens remembered the blood-stained division of the subcontinent and the nation's unfulfilled legacy.

In his speech to the midnight meeting of parliament, Narayanan appealed to citizens to mount a national movement to cleanse India of corruption and poverty, which he said had marred five decades of freedom.
Narayanan lauded India's achievements in maintaining unity, deepening democracy and promoting economic growth during its half century since winning independence.
But India's first low-caste president, who was elected to the mostly ceremonial post last month, urged citizens to reflect on the "shortcomings and failures" blocking progress.
"Here, though we have registered significant successes, the fact of the matter is that we have not been able to abolish poverty, ignorance and disease from among our people," he said.
Earlier, thousands of Indians waving flags and led by aged "freedom fighters" paraded through the heart of the capital.

Holding aloft the tricolour national flag, 75 men and women who led the struggle against British rule rode in open jeeps through throngs of people lining a boulevard called King's Way under colonial rule, now named Rajpath.
Many wore Nehru's trademark peaked white cotton cap.

Musicians played modern renditions of India's national song from a large stage set before the ornate presidential palace, its sandstone edges traced against the evening sky by strings of shimmering lights.
"Whatever language we speak, whatever clothes we wear, in whichever regions we live, we are all Indians," Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral told the crowd. "We are all one."
But a bomb blast triggered by militants in the troubled northeastern region earlier on Thursday was a violent reminder of India's continuing struggle against separatist violence.
Seven people were killed and eight injured when the device exploded on a train track in Assam state, derailing a carriage.
It was the latest attack in a mounting campaign of insurgency-related violence in the northeast, where dozens of separatist groups are fighting India rule.
The army, paramilitary units and police in the region, as well as in rebellious Kashmir and the capital New Delhi, tightened security ahead of independence celebrations.
